title: Cutting food waste in restaurants and shops
summary: A project run as a small business in a mid-sized European city helps restaurants, cafés and food shops waste less. It measures kitchen waste so businesses can cut it at the source, sells unavoidable surplus at a discount through an app, and passes what still doesn't sell to a food bank.
whyThisWorks: The problem says where the waste comes from and what it costs, without naming the app. The activities tackle waste in order: prevent it in the kitchen first, then rescue what's left. Because this is run as a business, the outcomes include covering its own costs, which investors and funders of social enterprises look for. The impact links to the EU's binding 2030 target. The assumptions name risks found in research: surplus food can still be wasted at home, and too many competing apps can backfire.

items: City restaurants and food shops throw away about 1 in 6 kg of the food they buy, mostly from over-ordering, large portions and unsold stock.
assumptions: Businesses act once they can see what they waste and what it costs

indicators.text: Food waste per meal served in partner kitchens
indicators.baseline: Set in each kitchen's first month of measuring
indicators.target: Tracked for context. Targets are set at outcome level.

items: Install waste-measuring scales in 40 restaurant kitchens
Send kitchens weekly reports on what they waste and its cost
Train kitchen staff on ordering, portions and using leftovers
Run an app selling surplus food at a discount at closing time
Pass food that still doesn't sell to a local food bank
assumptions: Enough businesses join to make the app worth using

indicators.text: Number of kitchens measuring their food waste
indicators.meansOfVerification: Device data, shared with businesses' consent

items: 40 kitchens measuring waste and receiving weekly reports
Staff in 40 kitchens trained on ordering and portions
150 restaurants and shops listing surplus on the app
Food bank collections three times a week
assumptions: Businesses keep measuring after the free trial ends
App fees stay affordable for small cafés

indicators.text: Businesses actively listing surplus each month

items: Kitchens order and prepare closer to what they sell
More surplus is sold or donated instead of thrown away
assumptions: Surplus bags match what customers can eat, so food isn't wasted at home

indicators.text: Kitchen food waste per meal served
indicators.baseline: 120 g per meal (first month of measuring)
indicators.target: 90 g per meal by the end of year 1

items: Partner businesses cut food waste by a quarter and save money
The business covers its costs from subscriptions and app fees
assumptions: Businesses don't cook extra just to fill app listings
Competing apps don't crowd the same small market

indicators.text: Average fall in partner kitchens' food waste
Share of the business's costs covered by its own revenue

items: City food businesses waste 30% less food per person by 2030
assumptions: City and national authorities keep measuring and reporting food waste

indicators.text: Food waste from the city's food businesses per resident
indicators.target: 30% lower by 2030, in line with EU targets
indicators.meansOfVerification: Municipal waste statistics reported under EU rules

draftPairs.improved: 40 kitchens measuring waste and receiving weekly reports
draftPairs.why: Reducing waste is a change in what restaurants do, so it's an outcome. An output is what the business delivers and can count directly.

draftPairs.improved: More surplus is sold or donated instead of thrown away
draftPairs.why: Selling surplus moves food out of the shop, but some can still be wasted at home, and research suggests too many competing apps can increase waste. The improved version claims only what the project can observe.
